old_title: Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobs
new_title: Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobs
old_text:
Nine of the 20 Premier League clubs will begin the 2026-27 season with a different man in the dugout than the one who ended the last campaign. Opta recently revealed that the only other seasons which started with so many men making their managerial debut for top flight clubs were 1888-89 and 1946-47; the inaugural season of league football and the first following the second world war. Neither occurred under normal circumstances yet the level of turnover this summer does not feel unusual. Job security has never meant less in the Premier League.
Adding in the recently appointed pair of Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick - confirmed in March and May respectively - means this season will start with 11 teams led by coaches with less than a year in their hotseat. The median tenure of Premier League managers at the start of each season has never been so low.
The most recent similar season was 2016-17. Heading into that campaign, 10 clubs had managers with under one year in the role. But with respect to the current Premier League crop, the relatively new head coaches that summer included Antonio Conte, Pep Guardiola, Jürgen Klopp and José Mourinho. All had either already won the Premier League or would go on to do so.
With Arsène Wenger still at Arsenal, four of those considered the five big beasts of Premier League management were competing, with the other (Alex Ferguson) having retired three years earlier. By contrast, Mikel Arteta is the only man who has won the English league who will be starting 2026-27 with the chance to do so again. There was also only one such manager two years ago, albeit it was Guardiola with his bulging trophy cabinet.
As Arteta has a single championship win, this season begins with the fewest English league titles on the division's collective CV in the Premier League era. The previous lowest at the beginning of a campaign was three in 1995-96 (thanks to Ferguson having two and Howard Wilkinson one) and 2019-20 (Guardiola two, Manuel Pellegrini one).
This is a natural byproduct of managers being younger and less experienced. The median age of Premier League managers is 46.9 years old. It was the same heading into 2024-25 but was last younger 20 years ago. The drop in age has not led to further opportunities for Englishmen.
Eddie Howe's departure from Newcastle means there will be three English managers when 2026-27 gets under way. The total was the same at the start of the last two campaigns, though interestingly it will be a different trio this year (Carrick, Frank Lampard and Gary O'Neil) than 12 months ago (Howe, Scott Parker and Graham Potter). The standing of the six clubs led by these men is worth considering. Two of the current coaches are at teams that have just been promoted, while two from last season's group were with sides that went on to be relegated. Opportunities with even relatively secure Premier League clubs are now rare for English managers, never mind at those with realistic title ambitions.
The top end of the division is likely to have a Spanish feel. The Basque region of Gipuzkoa is providing more head coaches to England's top division than England, with Arsenal, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Liverpool led by men from that relatively small area of Spain. It's plausible none of them will win the league given the presence of Manchester City (who themselves are under new management after a decade of Guardiola) but Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola are in charge of three of the leading four clubs in the title betting market, with Unai Emery's Villa seventh.
Managers from overseas lessening opportunities for English coaches in the Premier League is simply following the trend on the pitch. Just 8.6% of available minutes went to players from outside Britain or Ireland in 1992-93 yet a new high of 69.6% was reached last season. It is a truly global competition at every level, including ownership and sporting directors.
The influence of the latter on recruitment decisions has blurred the line between being a head coach and a manager. Liam Rosenior said he was "extremely humbled and honoured to be appointed head coach of Chelsea Football Club" when he was appointed by the Blues in January. "It fills me with immense pride to become manager of this great club," was Xabi Alonso's line when he secured essentially the same gig less than six months later. Based on the announcements clubs made to herald news of their appointments, the Premier League currently employs 14 head coaches and six managers.
Regardless of what the sign says on Alonso's office door, he should reflect upon his new club giving him a four-year contract when they haven't kept a manager for as long as two years since Conte left in 2018, or three years since Mourinho's first spell in charge over a decade earlier.
Rosenior learned this the hard way. He signed a six-and-a-half year deal yet Chelsea previously employed both Rafael Benítez and Guus Hiddink on interim bases for longer than the young Englishman lasted at the club. Head coach or manager, call it what you will. The profession has never offered shorter-term employment, or felt less English, in the Premier League.
